chapter_theme: In the council hall a counsellor presses the king with a theory of kingship: the king's heat or grace is the world's, the king and learning are its eyes, and austerity and rule are two hard burdens. Then, asking leave to speak of a maiden's lord, he turns to a long praise of the Vidyadhara realm as a heaven on the ridge.

cast.role: a counsellor in the council hall, speaking to the king; unnamed in these verses
the king addressed in the council hall, called lord of kings and bearer of the spear

263.reading: The counsellor says that if the sun scorched the great sea there would be no end to the misery of the creatures that live in its water, and so, when a king grows cruel and fierce, aram goes astray and the world suffers hard pain.

claims.claim: a cruel king throws aram into confusion and the whole world into suffering

264.reading: If kings give up the old way of guarding the earth's coolness and their white parasols grow hot, then even the cool ponds and groves, which flower to please the eye, will be scorched with them.

claims.claim: when the king abandons his duty to guard, the cool places of the land are scorched along with him

265.reading: If the king bent on evil will do nothing but destroy, the people have no refuge to go to; as the deer of the bamboo slopes fear the tiger, so the whole world is driven out.
265.nuance: The last two lines compare the people to deer driven from a tiger-haunted hill; the exact turn of line 4 is hard to fix.

claims.claim: a king who only destroys leaves his people no refuge

266.reading: When men wound one another, the only best thing for anyone is the shade at the feet of a king who stands in aram and guards the people like his own sweet life, watching that they not come to begging.

claims.claim: nothing is better for any people than the shelter of a king who stands in aram and guards them like his own life

267.reading: The counsellor says that, as the king orders a man's lot for both worlds in one act, there is no god so great as he, and calls him god-like on that ground; how the man's suffering and wealth are meant is not clear.
267.nuance: The word உம்மை (a former birth) is in line 1, so the verse seems to set a king's power beside the working out of earlier deeds, but the grammar of lines 1-2 allows more than one construction.

claims.claim: a king who shapes the lot of both worlds for his subjects is as great as a god, and no other deity is greater

268.reading: The counsellor names three eyes, the king, learning and the sun that circles the sky, and says that without the one set first among them nothing else could drive the darkness from the earth.
268.nuance: Which eye is meant by the one 'set at the head' (line 3) is not stated; the speaker's praise of the king in the preceding verses suggests the king, but it may also be learning.

claims.claim: the king, learning and the sun are the three eyes of the world

269.reading: The counsellor asks what the dwellers of the sky would say if the harsh rod, death and disease did not lie upon the people of the earth, and addresses the king as the lord of kings whom rulers bow to in turn.
269.nuance: The question in lines 1-2 is cut short and the sense of பயிறும் (practise, serve) is not fixed, so the point of the question is unclear.

270.reading: Not even the stars, shining like the cool moon in the sky, outshine men as kings do; no people in the world's bright round are greater than kings, says the counsellor to the angry elephant of a king.

claims.claim: no people on earth are greater than kings

271.reading: The two burdens of a king, hard austerity and the weight of rule, are each hard to bear and must be borne by hardship to himself, guarding life and bowing the mind; if either strays from its own work it brings great sorrow.

claims.claim: a king must bear both tapas and the burden of rule, each held to its proper work, or great sorrow follows

272.reading: Asked what ways lead to the rule of the gods and the sight of Indra's world, the counsellor says that the true word that never fails the mantra and great austerity are the ways, or else a king holding the sceptre in policy without slackening.
272.nuance: Two roads to the same world are put together: the ascetic's and the king's. The verse gives no word of grace; both depend on the doer's effort.

claims.claim: the world of the gods is reached through truth faithful to the mantra and great austerity, or through unslackening just rule

273.reading: Even a man who could lift a diamond hill on his strength to carry it far would find the two burdens, austerity and rule, hard to bear, the counsellor tells the lord of the great treasures given to beggars.

claims.claim: austerity and the burden of rule are harder to bear than lifting a mountain

274.reading: The counsellor says that, as a deed done by a man in an earlier birth rises into fruit and shows that it was real, the fruit of the counsel kings take comes out as they intend, and asks the king to say what he is thinking.
274.nuance: Karma is used as a comparison for counsel, not argued; the speaker treats it as known.
274.event: The counsellor asks the king to tell the plan he has in mind.

claims.claim: a deed of a former birth rises into fruit and shows that it was real

275.reading: Counsel, says the speaker, is like a pomegranate seed fed with cotton, whose form shows again in the blossom of its branch; he adds that he cannot say one harsh word.
275.nuance: The comparison is clear in outline, but how the seed's form returning in the flower fits counsel, and who is the subject of line 4, is not certain.

276.reading: The counsellor says that all the virtues told of kings gather and take form in the king before him, so whatever the counsellors say of the ways of policy will seem to men who have learned the books to their end like an old tale.

277.reading: The counsellor asks the king, if he will hear what he tells gladly of the lord fit for the maiden, to grant a little time.
277.nuance: Lines 1-3 name a maiden of sweet speech and coral lips and a lord fit for her; who is meant is not stated until later verses, and the reading of the clause is therefore open.
277.event: The counsellor asks for a little time to speak about the lord fit for the maiden.

278.reading: The counsellor begins to describe the northern hill, adorned for festival, where the Vidyadharas live, and says it is like a heaven in which the gods are never gone.
278.nuance: The speaker calls the hill the northern mountain (வடமலை); verse 130 places the city on the southern ridge.

279.reading: The counsellor says this realm is like the sky-world to the people of earth but hard for those without merit to enter, full of wishing-tree groves, and rich in heaven's pleasures.

claims.claim: those without merit cannot enter such a world

280.reading: The groves of the realm bear fruit in every season, wealth of every kind is gathered in it, and all troops of gods can enjoy all the senses there day and night.

281.reading: Lotuses with golden petals bloom in its ponds, golden garlands open in its groves, golden pollen covers its jewelled ground, and golden dust shines in the air.

282.reading: The groves are wishing-trees, the lovers' places are sandal bowers and the perfumes are musk and civet; the counsellor asks whether anything else could be called heavens.

283.reading: No hall there lacks jewels, its golden streams are past counting, and its gem hills cannot be numbered; the counsellor asks who would not be bound if he got them.

claims.claim: no one stays free of attachment once he has gained such riches

284.reading: Above it, the counsellor says, sixty great cities touch the sun's bright disk, and among the cities that cannot be left one shines like a crest-jewel under spreading moonlight.
284.nuance: சூளாமணி, the crest-jewel, is the name of the whole work; here the word is a comparison for one city.

285.reading: None of the mansions of that golden world is built of wood or clay, and a golden city called Ratna-pallavam surpasses the city of the old gods.
285.nuance: The initial of line 4 is garbled, and the identity of the city named (and its relation to the city of verse 130) is not clear.

286.reading: Women with bangled hands play with their men, desire sprouts endlessly in them, and the city seems a gods' world come down in joy, loud with its noise.

links.note: Kural 559 says that when a ruler bends justice the sky bends the rain; verse 263 says that a cruel king is to the world as a sea-scorching sun is to its creatures.
links.teaches: The Kural names rain as the lost gift, but the epic names the people's suffering as the creatures' in a burning sea, so the ruler's fault is one of heat, not drought.

gains.a: The measure of the loss: not a missed crop but life in a sea turned hostile, which the Kural's line does not give.
gains.b: A different figure for the same fault, in which the injured are creatures with nowhere to go, not a land that goes dry.

links.note: Kural 389 puts the world under the parasol of a king who can bear bitter words; verse 264 says that a parasol grown hot scorches the cool ponds and groves under it.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the cool shade as a gift of the king's patience, and the epic gives the reverse: when the king is hot the shade itself scorches.

gains.a: The danger the Kural leaves unsaid: shade turned to heat when the one under it loses his patience.
gains.b: A named cause of the parasol's coolness, the king's duty of guarding, in a parallel to the Kural's patience.

links.note: Verse 266 says that nothing is better for the world than the shade at the feet of a king who stands in aram and guards the people like his own life; verse 140 faults a king who has every virtue but lacks grace to the lowly.
links.teaches: The counsellor's ideal king guards all like his life, and the poet's own Vidyadhara king, perfect but lacking grace, shows the ideal cannot be taken as met by any one virtue.

links.note: Kural 544 says the world holds to the feet of the great king who embraces his people; verse 266 says no one has anything better than the shade of such a king's feet.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the king's embrace of his people the condition of the world's clinging to his feet, and the epic gives the reason: they cling because men are wounding one another.

gains.a: A cause for the clinging, which is men's mutual harm, where the couplet gives only the condition.
gains.b: A negative picture of what the world is like without the king's feet, which the couplet only implies.

links.note: Kural 388 calls the king who protects with justice the இறை of his people; verse 267 calls him god-like because he orders a man's lot in both worlds.
links.teaches: The epic gives a reason for the Kural's word இறை as god: his rule reaches the next world's lot as well as this one's, which the couplet leaves untouched.

gains.a: The ground for calling the king godlike, which is a claim about both worlds.
gains.b: A reading in which இறை means a power over a man's fortune and not only a title of rule.

links.note: Kural 392 says numbers and letters, learning, are the eyes of living beings; verse 268 names three eyes, the king, learning and the sun.
links.teaches: The Kural calls learning the only eye of life, and the epic puts learning beside the king and the sun, so what learning sees is made one of three lights the world needs.

gains.a: A rival that sees where learning cannot, the king, the sun's equal in lifting the world's darkness.
gains.b: A list that puts learning's eyes among the world's lights and not only life's.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 1006 says that worship brings Indra's wealth, then the siddhis, then release; verse 272 says the world of the gods is reached by the true word and great austerity or by unslackening rule.
links.teaches: The same prize, Indra's world, is reached by worship in one and by one's own austerity or rule in the other, so the paths differ over whether a god's favour is needed; the conflict holds if Tirumular's worship counts as asking his grace.

gains.a: A path that asks for no god: the epic's way depends on the doer's truth, austerity and rule.
gains.b: A way to see worship as one route among several to Indra's wealth, which the epic's king-or-ascetic choice does not need.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 1464 says kings of the just sceptre and countless great ascetics have fallen; verse 273 says austerity and rule are heavy burdens, harder than lifting a diamond hill.
links.teaches: The epic stresses how heavy the two burdens are, and Tirumular says that even those who bore both have fallen, so the weight is not the end of the road.

gains.a: A measure of the fall: the ones who fell had borne the hardest burdens.
gains.b: A sense of what the fallen kings and ascetics had carried before they fell.

links.note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out the one who did it as a calf finds its mother among many cows; verse 274 says a deed done in a former birth rises into fruit and shows that it was real.
links.teaches: The epic uses karma's sureness as the model for counsel, so a plan's result is as certain as a deed's fruit, a use of karma that the quatrain does not make.

gains.a: A comparison for the way a royal plan works, which turns karma into a model of policy.
gains.b: A second sign of how settled the doctrine is in Tamil verse, said in passing by a counsellor.

links.note: Naladiyar 137 doubts that the city of those in the wide heaven is sweeter than learned men gathering and laughing together; verse 279 praises a heaven-like realm that only the meritorious can enter.
links.teaches: The quatrain tests the heaven the epic praises against the pleasure of a company of the learned, and the epic's heaven is praised for its senses while the quatrain finds its sweetness no better than conversation.

gains.a: A measure to doubt its own claim: a pleasure the Naladiyar sets against heaven's.
gains.b: A full picture of the heaven it weighs, which is the one this verse and its neighbours describe.

links.note: Verse 129 ends the poet's praise of the ridge by asking what more need be told once its groves are wishing-tree gardens with golden lotuses; verse 282 ends on a question of the same kind.
links.teaches: The same closing question over wishing-tree groves is first the poet's boast and then the counsellor's pitch to the king, so the ridge's beauty is now used to move a decision.

links.note: Naladiyar 14 says a once-desired woman, bent and shaking on a staff, torments men who still desire her; verse 286 describes lovers whose desire sprouts without end in a heaven-like city.
links.teaches: The epic's desire without end belongs to a realm without death (278), so the quatrain's old age has no place there, which shows that the quatrain's argument depends on this world.

gains.a: A world where the quatrain's decline does not happen, and so a limit on the quatrain's lesson.
gains.b: A picture of the endless desire against which the quatrain's old woman is the corrective.

links.note: Verse 130 names a golden city, Ratanupura-Chakravalam, on the southern ridge; verse 285 names a golden city of Ratna-pallavam in the same realm.
links.teaches: The counsellor's golden city may be the poet's or a second one, so the king hears of the Vidyadhara country in terms that differ slightly from the poet's own.

source_issues: Verse 274 reads என்ணுவ for எண்ணுவ, a plain misprint.
Verse 285 line 4 begins with a stray ணி (ணிரத்தின), apparently a broken initial of தண் or the like.
Verse 271 line 3 reads செய்கையிர் றிரியு where செய்கையின் றிரியு is expected; this edition's sandhi is uneven.
Verses 263 and 282 carry an edition's question mark inside the verse.
Verses 278 to 286 are in shorter-lined quatrains in a different metre from 263 to 277, and the speaker is not marked as changing; they are read here as the counsellor's own description.
Verse 278 calls the hill the northern mountain (வடமலை), where verse 130 places the city on the southern ridge.
